patterns.detail: Sono is I or they. Sei is you. È is he, she or it. Siamo is we. Siete is you all. For other verbs, -o means I, -i means you, -e or -a means he, she or polite you. Session 10: heard "Mi porta" (you bring me, polite) as "he brings me", and "Non voglio zucchero" as "you do not want". Session 11: said "it arrives" for arrivo (I arrive), and mixed up esco, esci and esce. Session 12: heard arriva as "you arrive", vuole as "I would like", and mi aiuta as "he helps". Session 14: heard vorrei as "you want"; esce (polite you) was right; deve right as polite you. Session 18: heard vieni as "he, she comes", prende as "I'll take", and vuole as vuoi ("you want"; volere not counted that session). The ending tells you: -i you, -e he or she.
patterns.name: Which person is it?

patterns.detail: Le finestre is "the windows." Le porte is "the doors." Missed in session 2, right in session 3, not tested since.
patterns.name: More than one: le with an -e ending

patterns.detail: Learned in session 13: sto tagliando (I am cutting), sto sbucciando (I am peeling), sto studiando. Sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno change with the person; the -ando or -endo word stays the same.
patterns.name: Saying what you are doing now: sto + -ando / -endo

patterns.detail: Italian often puts the verb first and the person after: Viene anche tuo fratello? = Comes also your brother? (Is your brother coming too?). Idea from session 15: a voice drill where the tutor says normal English and you say it in Italian word order, still in English.
patterns.name: Italian word order
